paragraphs: I think that in no country in the civilized world is less attention paid to philosophy than in the United States. The Americans have no philosophical school of their own, and they care very little about the schools into which Europe is divided, whose very names are scarcely known to them. Nevertheless, it is easy to see that almost all the inhabitants of the United States use their understanding in the same way and govern it by the same rules. That is, without ever having taken the trouble to define the rules of a philosophical method, they possess one, common to the whole people. They avoid the bondage of system and habit, of family maxims, class opinions, and to some degree national prejudices. They accept tradition only as a means of information, and existing facts only as a lesson for doing things differently and better. They seek the reason of things for themselves, and in themselves alone. They aim at results without being tied to means, and at the substance through the form. Such are the principal characteristics of what I shall call the philosophical method of the Americans. But if I go further and look among these characteristics for the one that predominates over almost all the rest and includes them, I find that in most operations of the mind each American appeals only to the individual exercise of his own understanding. America is therefore one of the countries in the world where philosophy is least studied and where the precepts of Descartes are best applied. Nor is this surprising. The Americans do not read the works of Descartes, because their social condition deters them from speculative studies, but they follow his maxims because this same social condition naturally disposes their understanding to adopt them. In the continual movement that stirs a democratic community, the tie that unites one generation to another is loosened or broken. Every man readily loses the trace of the ideas of his forefathers or takes no care about them. Nor can people living in this state of society draw their beliefs from the opinions of the class to which they belong, for, so to speak, there are no longer any classes, or those that still exist are made up of such mobile elements that the body can never exercise real control over its members. As for the influence that one man’s intelligence has on another’s, it must necessarily be very limited in a country where the citizens, placed on a footing of general similarity, all see one another closely, and where, since no signs of incontestable greatness or superiority are seen in any one of them, they are constantly brought back to their own reason as the most obvious and nearest source of truth. What is destroyed then is not only confidence in this or that man, but the taste for trusting the ipse dixit of any man whatsoever. Everyone shuts himself up in his own breast and from there claims to judge the world.

The practice among the Americans of fixing the standard of their judgment in themselves alone leads them to other habits of mind. Since they see that they manage to resolve without assistance all the little difficulties that their practical life presents, they readily conclude that everything in the world can be explained and that nothing in it goes beyond the limits of the understanding. Thus they end up denying what they cannot comprehend. This leaves them little faith in whatever is extraordinary and an almost insurmountable distaste for whatever is supernatural. As they are accustomed to rely on their own testimony, they like to see the object that engages their attention with extreme clearness. They therefore strip away as much as possible of all that covers it, rid themselves of whatever separates them from it, and remove whatever hides it from sight, in order to view it more closely and in the broad light of day. This disposition of mind soon leads them to despise forms, which they regard as useless and inconvenient veils placed between them and the truth.

The Americans, then, have not needed to draw their philosophical method from books; they have found it in themselves. The same thing can be observed in what has happened in Europe. This same method has been established and made popular in Europe only to the degree that the condition of society has become more equal and people have grown more like each other. Let us consider for a moment how the periods in which this change can be traced are connected. In the sixteenth century the Reformers subjected some of the dogmas of the ancient faith to the scrutiny of private judgment, but they still withheld all the rest from it. In the seventeenth century, Bacon in the natural sciences and Descartes in philosophy in the strict sense abolished accepted formulas, destroyed the empire of tradition, and overthrew the authority of the schools. The philosophers of the eighteenth century finally generalized the same principle and undertook to submit to the private judgment of each man all the objects of his belief.

Who does not see that Luther, Descartes, and Voltaire used the same method, and that they differed only in how far each said it should be applied? Why did the Reformers keep so closely within the circle of religious ideas? Why did Descartes, who chose to apply his method only to certain matters even though he had made it fit for all, declare that men might judge for themselves in matters philosophical but not in matters political? How did it happen that in the eighteenth century those general applications were suddenly drawn from this same method, which Descartes and his predecessors had either not noticed or had rejected? And finally, how are we to explain that at this period the method we are speaking of suddenly left the schools, entered society, and became the common standard of intelligence; and that, once it had become popular among the French, it was openly adopted or secretly followed by all the nations of Europe?

The philosophical method described here may have been produced in the sixteenth century; it may have been more accurately defined and more widely applied in the seventeenth. But in neither century could it be commonly adopted. Political laws, the condition of society, and the habits of mind that derive from these causes were still opposed to it. It was discovered at a time when men were beginning to equalize and assimilate their conditions. It could be generally followed only in ages when those conditions had at last become nearly equal and men nearly alike.

The philosophical method of the eighteenth century is therefore not only French but democratic, and this explains why it was so readily accepted throughout Europe, where it has contributed so powerfully to changing the face of society. The French did not convulse the world because they changed their former opinions and altered their former customs. They did so because they were the first to generalize and bring to light a philosophical method that made it easy to attack all that was old and to open a path to all that was new.

If it is asked why this same method is today more rigorously followed and more frequently applied by the French than by the Americans, although the principle of equality is no less complete among the latter and is of more ancient date, the fact may be attributed to two circumstances, which it is essential to understand clearly at the outset. It must never be forgotten that religion gave birth to Anglo-American society. In the United States, therefore, religion is blended with all the habits of the nation and all the feelings of patriotism, and this gives it a particular force. To this powerful reason another of no less intensity may be added: in America religion has, as it were, set its own limits. Religious institutions have remained wholly distinct from political institutions, so that former laws have been easily changed while former belief has remained unshaken. Christianity has therefore kept a strong hold on the public mind in America. I would particularly remark that its sway is not only that of a philosophical doctrine adopted after inquiry, but of a religion that is believed without discussion. In the United States Christian sects are infinitely diversified and perpetually modified, but Christianity itself is a fact so irresistibly established that no one undertakes either to attack or to defend it. The Americans, having accepted the principal doctrines of the Christian religion without inquiry, are obliged to accept in the same way a great number of moral truths that originate in it and are connected with it. Hence the activity of individual analysis is restrained within narrow limits, and many of the most important human opinions are removed from its influence.

The second circumstance I mentioned is this: the social condition and the constitution of the Americans are democratic, but they have not had a democratic revolution. They arrived on the soil they now occupy in almost the condition in which we see them today, and this matters a great deal.

No revolution fails to shake existing belief, weaken authority, and cast doubt on commonly received ideas. The effect of all revolutions is therefore, more or less, to surrender men to their own guidance and to open to the mind of every man a void and almost unlimited range of speculation. When equality of conditions follows a protracted conflict between the different classes that made up the older society, envy, hatred, and uncharitableness, pride, and exaggerated self-confidence tend to seize the human heart and hold sway there for a time. Independently of equality itself, this tends powerfully to divide men — to lead them to mistrust the judgment of others and to seek the light of truth nowhere but in their own understandings. Everyone then tries to be his own sufficient guide and makes it his boast to form his own opinions on all subjects. Men are no longer bound together by ideas but by interests, and it would seem that human opinions are reduced to a kind of intellectual dust, scattered on every side, unable to collect, unable to cohere.

Thus the independence of mind that equality presupposes is never so great, and never seems so excessive, as when equality is beginning to establish itself and during the painful labor by which it is established. The kind of intellectual freedom that equality may give must therefore be very carefully distinguished from the anarchy that revolution brings. Each of these two things must be considered separately, so as not to form exaggerated hopes or fears about the future.

I believe that people living under the new forms of society will often use their private judgment, but I am far from thinking that they will often abuse it. This is due to a cause that applies more generally to all democratic countries, and that in the long run must keep the independence of individual speculation within fixed, and sometimes narrow, limits. I shall point out this cause in the next chapter.
